utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are all here except Ms. Nikolic. The rest are all here. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. I understand that -- rather before I give you the floor, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey - I understand that you have a preliminary to raise - two things. Mr. Bourgon, has the joint response on the protective measures being filed or are we going to have it today? Can you inform us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Our understanding that this response, Joint Defence Response, has indeed been filed and a courtesy copy I understand was also given to the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The other thing is this: Yesterday, when we wound up for the time being the testimony of Major Rutten, I asked him to liaise with the VW unit and also the registrar, to inquire about his possible return. Could we have the dates, if we have them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've been informed that Major Rutten will be available Thursday, 7 of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you go around that and reschedule your timetable or your plan to witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfect with us, Your Honour, and we can work with that date, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. And the understanding is that the documents will be tendered when he finishes his testimony, all right? Okay. So we have an understanding on that. There is, I understand, a preliminary that the Prosecution would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours. I have a little bit of housekeeping before this witness comes in. In the packet, which I believe has been passed out to you, related to this witness there are two mistakes which we fixed but I wanted to alert everybody and I've told my friends on the other side. Tab two, our index, the date is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me just follow you. Tab 2, where is the mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The date column, it should be 27 July, not 26 July. That's our error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the index?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be on the cover, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. So can you repeat, Mr. Nicholls, again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. The date for tab 2 on the index should be 27 July, not 26 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we have inserted pages 00727972 through 7974 to make that clear, and those -- through 75, excuse me -- and those pages have also been passed out to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The second error is that tab 3 is not in fact an intercept taken by this witness, that's 65 ter number 1361. So I will not be discussing that today. It's not his intercept. I'm sorry for these errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last point is I wanted to just address the Court briefly on our plan for future intercept operators. We want to have an -- an abbreviated direct for these witnesses, as most of them will be 92 ter. And rather than have of them look at their handwriting for each and every intercept - some of them have many - we plan to give them the packet before they testify and have them check, and then ask then if they have checked through the packet and ask them whether, in fact, the handwritten intercepts in there are their intercepts, which they transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that the -- a copy of the packet would be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. It would be the same packet, and we might have them initial the pages they've reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you could also make it clear with the various witnesses that they need to bring over with them the packet in case any one wants to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We will have the packet with us in court after they've reviewed it in our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in addition, we plan to do an abbreviated background direct with them and ask them, where they were working, if they followed the procedures of that location, and then we will go into discussing one or more of the intercepts but probably not each and every intercept in the packet. That's just in an effort to speed things up with the operators who were not in any kind of a supervisory role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any comments from any of the Defence teams on this? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. The only comment I have, and maybe since we are in the housekeeping mode, is that we would like to have a status of the statements that these intercept operators gave to the Dutch authorities. A couple of them, I think, as we've heard, are actually -- gave statements without obtaining a pseudonym or any confidential status; others, though, did retain their confidential status that we saw. It was similar to the DutchBat witnesses so I know I've spoken to my learned friends a couple times about that, and we would like to get their statements so that we can have at least a complete set of information that these witnesses provided to all the authorities, not just the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we are working on that. It doesn't arise with the next witness but I believe we are trying -- I don't know what stage we are at but we are trying to get all of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to make sure that the Defence teams have got as complete a picture as possible. Please try to ensure that the Defence has at their disposal as complete a picture as possible before each witness belonging to there category turns up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, thank you. Any further -- any further remarks? None. Let me just tell you what's going to happen today. We'll have the first break as usual, at 3.45, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00. Then we'll break a couple of minutes before 5.30. As I explained to you yesterday, we have an extraordinary plenary of judges, and we all need to be there for, I reckon, I'll try to contain our presence for half an hour. Then we hope to return here at 6.00 and we'll have the last session which will run to 7.00. All right? So break at 3.45 and another one at 5.30 or thereabouts. Okay. Next witness has a pseudonym and facial distortion. Thank you. Now, how long do you plan your examination-in-chief to last, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm hoping I can do it in about an hour and a half, maybe slightly longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically we are saying that -- do we have an indication from the Defence? I think we have. How long is that going to last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal and also the Trial Chamber I should like to welcome you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a witness brought forward by the Prosecution in this case which deals with the events of July 1995 in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You testified already in Krstic, in the Krstic case, and on that occasion, you were granted two protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym instead of your usual name, and surname, and also facial distortion. We have kept those protective measures in force and they will be applicable also throughout your testimony in this trial. I take it you have been explained already what this means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make sure that you are satisfied with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls for the Office of the Prosecutor will be summarising the testimony you gave in Krstic and then proceed with some questions, and he will then be followed by the seven Defence teams who will be -- which will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that you will be with us here today and also tomorrow, and let's hope that we'll try and finish with your testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I have some help from the usher to show the witness the pseudonym sheet? Could you please slow it to Defence counsel as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please just take a look at what's written on the piece of paper you're being handed. Don't read it out loud but could you confirm that your name is written on that piece of paper along with PW 130?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, that is my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P02313 under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the first thing I want to ask you about, sir, is your review of your testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Sorry to interrupt you like this with your very first question. I want to avoid confusion. In the confidential Prosecution exhibits list intended for this witness, the pseudonym sheet is marked as 2314, 2313 would be the testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As usual. So let's, for the purpose of the record, change that, all right? The pseudonym list -- sheet will be 2314 and not 2313. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: With the assistance of an interpreter, sir, who read it to you, did you review the entire transcript of your testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you made the following corrections: On page 8798 of that transcript, at line 11, "Srebrenica" should have been written as "Srebrenik," and on line 13 of that same page, "Ranovici," should have been written as "Banovici." And on page 8799, at line 3, the word "from" should have been the word "until." Now, other than those few corrections, do you attest that the transcript of your testimony in the Krstic trial accurately reflects what you stated in that trial, and that your answers would be the same if you were asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Fully, yes, I agree. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go into private session, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Open session].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness has been a ham radio operator and enthusiast since he was ten years old. From June 1993 the witness served as a member of the intercept unit for the 2nd Corps, the EPD later known as the PEB. He started in June before his official appointment. The witness has assigned to a location where he was a platoon leader of two squads. His rank beginning in 1994 was lieutenant. In the Krstic trial, the witness discussed three specific intercepts. The witness in his testimony recognised his handwriting in one of the notebooks used by the intercept operators. This was notebook number 231, Exhibit 844 in the Krstic case, 65 ter number 02315 in this case. In this notebook, the witness recognised his handwriting for intercepts recorded on the 2nd of August 1995, at 12.40 and 1300 hours and we will be looking at those intercepts today. The witness also recognised the printouts of these two conversations which were Krstic exhibits 850A; 1392 in this case. And 853A in Krstic; 1395 in this case. The witness also testified about a conversation between General Krstic and a person named Mandzuka, recorded in handwritten notebook number 103. That was Krstic P747, 65 ter number 1065 in this case. That intercept occurred on the 2nd of August 1995 at 10.00 a.m. The witness was able to determine the date of this intercept based on his review of the printed copy of the intercept. Krstic Exhibit P862A, which is 1389 in this case. That intercept at 10.00 a.m. Was not recorded in the handwritten notebook by this witness but by a different operator. Going back to the later exhibit, intercept, from that day, August 2nd, 1995 at 1300, between Krstic and Popovic, the witness confirmed in his Krstic testimony that he had listened to the audio tape recording of this conversation in the office of the OTP. And the witness confirmed that it was he who recorded this conversation and transcribed it in his handwriting from the tape to the notebook. The witness recognised and recalled the audio tape recording which is Krstic Exhibit P854, again 1395 in this case, as the conversation he transcribed into the notebook and, Your Honours, with the Court's permission, I will be playing that recording later on in the witness's testimony. That's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've got some questions for you now, sir. It's correct, isn't it, that you reviewed in our offices a binder with five handwritten intercepts in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also reviewed the original notebooks containing those handwritten intercepts which are copied into the folder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were able to confirm that the intercepts under tabs 1, 2, 4, and 5, were all transcribed by you and you recognised your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you will also able to tell me that the intercept at tab 3, dated 26 July, 1995, at 1537, was not in your handwriting, that was not one of your intercepts and you did not transcribe that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we briefly go back into private session for some background questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, beginning the time after November 1993, how many men were in the two squads of your platoon in the south location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop for a moment. I'm not receiving any interpretation. I don't know about the others. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I kindly ask you to give your answer again from the beginning because we were not receiving interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask to remind the witness not to say the name of the location, which I think he may have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But if he has, then let's have a broadcast redaction. Okay? Broadcast redaction, because that becomes important. We don't need to redact anything from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After November 1993, how many men were in the two squads of your platoon at the south location?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And is that the same amount of men who would have been working in July of 1995 at this location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, we are going to get stuck if we proceed like this. Already we have thrown away five more minutes because the next break will be -- need to be of 30 minutes instead of the 25 that I had planned. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I had just asked you the amount of men working in July 1995, was that the same as you've just described, nine men in each squad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, on the outside, there were nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, once these men became part of the platoon, did they receive any additional training from you in their tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's only natural for them, to be able to work. They had to be given training for that job. True enough, these were men who were youngish, but who had undergone training and who had taken certain tests in radio amateur activity, so they found their way quite quickly and learnt quickly so that they didn't need a great deal of training. They simply needed to have the system and the principles explained and they would adopt that quickly and they worked efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And very briefly, as you saw it, what were your principal duties, your most important duties, as commander of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I understood my duties, or rather I never saw myself as a member of the army. I never in my life thought that I would have to engage in that sort of activity. These were mostly young men of the same age as my daughter, so I saw them as my children, and working with them, I never treated them as a senior officer or commander but simply as a friend so that we would work together, and throughout the period that we did work together there were any never any problems or excesses or any unpleasantness whatsoever so that everything functioned normally. We had a common interest in doing the job as well as we could. I also was duty-bound to take care of supplies, with communication means, and in many situations I had to repair certain faults on the spot, on the equipment, and to make improvements so that we could work better so that there was a wide spectrum of activities that I engaged in, and in addition to all those duties as the squad leader, I also worked on an equal footing with the others. I took part in shifts together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I was always punctual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, what is your assessment of the performance of the men during 1995 who you were working with? You've already said how it was a very good working relationship but how well did you feel they were doing their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I never had any objections to their work. Everybody worked very hard, and there was no situation when we had any kind of dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many shifts were there during a 24 hour period at the location where you were commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, most often we worked in six-hour shifts. That is to say four shifts over 24 hours. However, in situations when it was cold, we would work shorter hours because we didn't have electricity regularly in all our rooms so sometimes we'd cut the working hours shorter, but in principle, it was six-hour work shifts, 6.00 in the morning, 12.00 noon, 12.00 in the evening, 6.00 p.m., that was the system of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during July 1995, were the shifts interrupted or were you able to work regular shifts, full shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: In that period, we could work quite normally without any hindrance and without any interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you describe, just so we get a picture, the facility or the lay out of the room used by the intercept operators at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, since in the month of May 1992, this facility was devastated when the army of Yugoslavia left, the then army of Yugoslavia, part of the facility was therefore unusable so we couldn't use the entire building and were therefore forced to place our equipment and the system in a smallish room. We had a room where we stayed, sort of a bigger one, and, of course, we had a room where we slept and we had a bathroom. However, in 1994, the facility was renovated so the other rooms could be used again. As for the equipment, the system that we used for intercepts were concerned, then we moved all of them into a bigger room, considerably bigger, which made it possible for us to work normally. However, we were not separated. We were all in the same room regardless of whether we were in the smaller room or in the bigger room. All the equipment was there and that's where the operators were. The operators who worked on this job, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before you and your men were using this site to intercept communications, what had it been used for before? What was the purpose of that facility before it began to be used by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, this facility was the main radio relay centre of the army of Yugoslavia, from where it operated for the entire territory, radio relay communications for meeting its own needs. I know that full well because, before the war, as members of the radio club for at least 20 years, we would go out to that elevation, given the approval of that army, and the state Secretariat, that is where we had our ham radio competitions at national level, international level. We had very good relations with the people there, with the army there actually. So we knew full well what was being done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, besides the men under your command in your unit, were there any other units present in 1995 working out of that facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, at that facility, there were security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's play it safe. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to start talking about the process of what you and your men were doing in intercepting communications but first if you can in a few words briefly tell us, and there is rather a general question but what was the purpose of monitoring VRS communications? What was the most important purpose or goal of there task you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, since at this south facility, southern facility, we had actually been there for 20 years or so before all of these things that started happening from 1992 until 1995. Both I and the rest knew full well what this elevation can do for us and what we can get done there. If you look at the map, too, you can see that it is an open facility. To the north, south, east and west. That is to say there are no natural obstacles. There are no impediments. So quite simply we tried to get some work done there and we saw that it could work, so the point was to intercept the radio relay communications of the army of Republika Srpska, and that is to say that we organised our work accordingly and we did that. It is a fact that we listened to radio relay communications and the radio relay centre which meant that we were listening to the top echelons of the command, high ranking officers. We did not go into lower-ranking units. That's what people did at direct lines of contact. We weren't interested in that. We intercepted the conversations of the Presidency of the RS, then the command, and so on and so forth. So I'm talking about those levels, brigades, corps, so on, those communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to show you some photos now and see if you can recognise them. And the first one is P02298. All right. Just take a moment to look at that. You should have a photo in front of you with the picture of some antennas on it. Can you take a look at that and tell me if you recognise the objects at the top of these towers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I recognise the objects because I was there. Well, this is not at the facility where I was commander. This is at the northern facility. It's antennae actually. I see two of them that actually followed the radio relay devices, the 800 ones. I see this particular antenna that followed the communication at the level of number 1, that's considerably lower than 800. We can talk about that in greater detail if you like. Then I see this antenna that was used for a different kind of communication at ultra-short communications, two metres. What should I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, this is of no help to us because he keeps saying this and that and this and that and I don't know exactly which is which. So I can at least distinguish four antennae, if not five, on this -- in this photo. If you could deal with them one by one, please, starting with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have the help of the usher to show the witness where the stylus is and we can just quickly mark the two that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Start with the dish first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you move left or right and just mark a number 1 by the dish on the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that one RRU-800 or the lower level RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: This was the 800 one. It's a parabolical antenna. I know that, Siemens made. I know the factory. It's a professional antenna that was used by the army of Yugoslavia at radio relay centres, everywhere throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that enabled communication between the radio relay centres of the military and that is how they maintained their communications. This antenna consists of a pass such element or reflector. It's the dish here. And in the middle - you see that there? - that's the so-called illuminator, and that is where the antenna is actually put. So it's a few curves that has a diameter depends on the frequency. It's a broad-band antenna, from 630 to 960 megahertz, from 630 to 960 megahertz. Let's move on. The second antenna, number 2, was also used for the same purpose. It's a professional Siemens antenna as well that was also used for the same purposes, except that it's not as strong as the first one. It is only natural that a bigger surface can take more signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, just a minute. You're going into a lot of detail, which is good, but it's probably to some extent more than, at least, I can understand completely. These two antennas, could they be directed towards different areas in order to pick up signals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You can see here that one is directed in one direction and the other one in a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, now if you could move on to number 3 on the right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to number 3 the one down here the red and white one. You see it here? This is the so-called log period antenna, the fish bone one. That's -- it's sort of a popular name because it is vaguely reminiscent of that. It's red and white here but this is an antenna that we used. I don't know. At our facility we also had these antennae, since we didn't have enough material. This is actually equipment that is used by experts in geometry. They are made of aluminium of 25-millimetre diameter, and they can be used for making broadband antennae too. When I say "broadband," I mean at least 200 or 300 megahertz. So it's not an antenna that receives only a single range but a broader range. So it's RRU-1, and the frequency it uses is from 170 to 230 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you are also seeking in this process to bring out the expertise of the witness, I would suggest that you direct him to just indicate the aerial and the use for which it was made at the time, without further details, because otherwise we'll never finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One question on number 3, the fish bone, was that one that was, I'll say "homemade," one that was built by your units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We used it at our facility too. We made them. I already mentioned that. I'm sure that they did it at this facility, too. I know, because these are not professional antennae. They were sort of make-shift antenna, homemade, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then if the next two on the right, which would be 4 and 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are three on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or 3. If you could mark those, sir, are those all RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: No. Perhaps the fourth one -- well, it looks like a fish bone antenna to me, so possibly -- well, it's a bit blurred so I can't see whether the elements are longer or shorter because that is what shows what type of antenna it is. So I cannot say for sure, but antenna number 4, as I marked it, that is a regular type antenna directed and it's not a broadband antenna. It was probably used for a particular type of ultra-short communication with radio stations emitting a particular type of signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you could just write perhaps in the bottom left-hand corner PW 130?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we capture that? Is that still part of the image? Okay. If we could go to the next photo, P02299.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very simply, sir, do you recognise this photo as another shot of a couple of the antennas we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. But the picture was taken from further down. That's what we were explaining a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally P02300. Again, are you able to recognise that as a photo of one of the antennae at the northern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the same thing that a few moments ago we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could go to P02301? Take a look at that photo for a minute, sir, and tell me if you can very simply what type of antenna that is and if you recognise the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. This is an antenna for working on RR-800. It's the same one that I explained a few moments ago, parabolical with an illuminator, and so on and so forth. This is the southern facility. This is no longer the northern facility. This is now the southern facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how can you tell it's the southern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, because this concrete holder of the antenna was used in the former Yugoslav People's Army. That is where they placed their antennae. I know the facility. I've known it for over 30 years. So I mean, I know very well what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have P02302, please? And that looks like there were several antenna here sir but without explaining them all, can you tell me where -- which facility these antennas were attached to, where they were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: This is also the southern facility. I just omitted to mention a moment ago that this concrete wall is on the roof of the southern facility, so there is this concrete belt all around it, where all these antennae were. Now I don't know exactly how many there were but there were quite a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next one, 2303, please. Same question, sir. Is that an antenna located at the southern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. This is the antenna that was at the southern facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 2304, please, the next one. Same question, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. This is an antenna that was also at the southern facility, that I made myself with my very own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Give me one minute to discuss something with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We think we can safely go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is the last photo of an antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You just explained to us that this was one that you built yourself out of -- it looks like a sign or something. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Because since there was a shortage of material, aluminium and what have you not, I used a traffic sign here as a reflector for this antenna and it is a particular type of antenna, and I did the calculations for it, and it was used -- well, I think that to this day, it's up there at that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can take that off the screen. Now, you mentioned these antennas could be directed. Did your platoon receive orders from the 2nd Corps in Tuzla which direction or azimuth in which to point the antennas or direct the antennas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, it's only logical; after all, we were a unit of the 2nd Corps. We worked for the 2nd Corps. And it is only natural that from our superior in the corps, the chief there and the commander of the company, we received our orders because we did not know how the situation was developing on the ground. They were following that and they knew from which directions they needed information, and then, quite simply, they would order us to turn the antennae in such and such a direction, using such and such an azimuth, so that's what we did. And we intercepted certain communications or rather certain conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you -- in July 1995, if you recall, which direction were your antennas directed or which general azimuth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: In principle, throughout this period, from this facility, we would monitor the area of eastern Bosnia where the Drina Corps was active, with its subordinate units, and occasionally, we had some other directions, but at least one of the radio relay devices was directed in that direction, so that we followed what was happening round the clock, all the communications that the Supreme Command of the Bosnian Serb army had. If I need to explain what an azimuth is, it is an angle between the direction of the north covered by the antenna, from the direction north. So it's an angle when you wish to monitor a particular radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did your platoon also receive orders from the 2nd Corps of which specific frequencies to monitor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally. But at my facility, it was my duty, and also I needed not every day but every two or three days to take a receiver, to review the entire frequency area, to see whether a new radio relay station had cropped up. If it had, then I would report that to the command and then they would decide whether any of them had to be monitored or not. Because they were not in a position to know what can be heard and what not, so they couldn't tell us in advance. Sometimes they would give us orders. If they expected certain operations in a particular area, they would say, "Listen in now," and then I would monitor that particular direction, to see whether anything could be heard or not, and then, if it could, I would ask them whether we should monitor it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In July 1995, were you familiar with the code names used for the various VRS units in the area you were monitoring that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I was not familiar with all of them, and this was not something that I was particularly interested in but I still remember some of them, like Domar, Prostor 99, I'm afraid it's a bit hard for me to remember right now but in any event, every brigade, whether it was the Zvornik or Bratunac or Milici or Sekovici Brigade, each of them had its own code name, such as those I mentioned a moment ago. But after so much time, I'm afraid I can't remember the names of each of those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right. I want to ask you now about very briefly about the equipment you were using to monitor communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we look at 1925 first, please? All right. Take a moment to look at that photo and tell me if you recognise that equipment, or perhaps not these exact electronic components but this type of equipment, and if you can tell me whether this type of equipment was in use at your facility, and, again, if you could just describe what these three different pieces do very briefly and number them 1, 2, 3, so we know which piece of equipment you're describing, and you could start with the largest piece, perhaps, on the front, towards the front of the photo, with the big circular dial. Mark that number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What is that piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: That is a short wave radio receiver which receives and transmits frequencies ranging from 2 megahertz to 30 megahertz. You can see that it is a Kenwood brand. It is a professional piece of equipment used by radio amateurs for their communications and also used by many other services who need to have communications on shortwaves. True, when you buy such devices, they have the other frequencies except radio amateur frequencies are blocked, but it is easy to contact Kenwood and to find out from them what you have to do to de-block the device for it to be able to receive the whole short wave spectrum, to listen in and to emit. This is Kenwood TS-450. I know that. You can't see that but that is the model. And it is the device that we had at our facility and that we used in our work. Number 2, here, is a radio device by the ICOM brand, R-100. It is just a receiver. So it can only listen, and this device covers the frequency from 30 megahertz to 1.7 gigahertz. So this was a device with the help of which we listened in to radio relay stations which are from 630 to 960 megahertz. So this device covered that range. And behind this big piece of equipment you will see a box which is a mixer for a high frequency, from 630 to 960 to be recorded on a radio relay device, and to be able to transfer it to the short-wave device, you had to mix the frequencies and reduce it to 4 megahertz for the short wave range and this device has one memory with four submemories, each of which can memorise up to 100 channels and it can scan each of those memories separately or all of them together, or only a particular number of channels that we wanted to monitor. And as RU-800 had 24 channels, we would deposit them in one of those memories so that we could receive that radio relay station fully. The speed can be adjusted by scanning. So all those 24 channels can pass through in two or three seconds. You listen in briefly. If there is a signal, you can hear it, you hear a sound, you stop the scanning, you rewind, and find that particular conversation, and then there is a tape recorder which is not shown here, and that tape recorder will record the conversation automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just label the mixer number 3 and we'll be done with this photo. Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at the bottom, could you just write PW-130, your pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We are through with that one. I'd like to now show you three photos of different recording devices and you tell me if you're familiar with them, if they are the type you used at your location. The first is 1926. That's not the number I had but we can go with that one, if that's 1926. Do you recognise that? And I think we need to rotate it 180 degrees. It is 1926. Do you recognise this type of equipment, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. This is a tape recorder, the brand is UHER, and we used it at our facility. We had several such devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you two more photos. P02306, please. If we could turn that one around as well, please? Again, sir, do you recognise this equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. It is also one of the tape recorders that we used for recording conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And lastly, 2307, the next one, please. Same question, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it is the same type of tape recorder that was also used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the -- thank you, I'm through with that. The monitoring equipment we saw, the Kenwood and the mixer and the receiver and these tape recorders, very briefly, who maintained and repaired that equipment as necessary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: There weren't really any major breakdowns but in my unit, there was a small section of two or three men who worked on the repairing of these devices. However, when it came to this mixer that I marked with the number 3, I did that. I took care of it. If necessary, I did the repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Should we break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have only got about two or three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many sets in July 1995 were in operation in the intercept room at your facility? In other words, how many sets where somebody could monitor and then record, using the equipment we've just gone through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: We had two sets for monitoring radio relay centres, RR-800. We had one set for RR-1, and if necessary, we could prepare another set, that is solely a receiver. That was more of a radio link than a radio relay link. So we had a maximum of four workplaces. They were very close to one another. So if there wasn't a lot of activity, one operator could cover two such sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 30-minute break. That means we'll resume at 4.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are proceeding with this sitting, as you would have noticed, invoking Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole cannot be with us, at least until the next session at 6.00. So let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We were talking about the sets in July 1995. You had two sets for monitoring radio relays -- centres RR-800. Was there a difference in the types of units of the VRS which used RR-800 as opposed to RRU-1? In other words, did a certain type of unit use one or other system?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Usually they would have one system -- one or other system. They always had RRU-800 at their disposal. That is the higher level units, whereas the lower level units frequently used RRU-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to move on to the topic of how the men in your platoon actually intercepted and recorded conversations from your location. And you already started telling us about this, how the men would -- when they heard a signal, would stop the scanning process and turn back to get to the channel they had heard. Could you briefly take us step by step through the process of what happens when an intercept operator detects a conversation in his headphones as he's scanning the airwaves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, let me continue. From the moment when during scanning you would hear a sound in the headphones or the loud-speaker, because the operators had headphones which they could wear to hear better, they would stop the scanning, they would wind back to -- buy two or three channels to find the channel on which the conversation is, and automatically they would switch on the tape recorder and start the recording. There is a button which says "pause," so you just de-block the pause button by pressing it and then the tape recorder automatically records that particular conversation. Once the conversation has been recorded, depending on whether there are more conversations on that same frequency or not, the operator sometimes couldn't and sometimes it wasn't necessary for him to immediately transcribe that conversation from the tape to the notebook. If it was urgent, then one of us, who was free, who could take over that part of the job, that is if it was urgent, the transcript could be done immediately and then it would be forwarded on. If it wasn't urgent, then the operator at the end of his shift would plan an hour or two at the end of his working hours to transcribe the conversations that we had decided to send to the corps command. We didn't send all of them because many were insignificant, irrelevant. They didn't require processing. So we didn't even make a record of such conversations. But one such a conversation is transcribed from the tape recorder to the notebook, then it would be retyped from the notebook on a computer. This would usually be done by the same operator or we also had an assistant who preferred to work with a computer and he would type out the conversation, and then this would be sent on to the command and -- for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We will talk about that in a minute. Thank you for explaining that. When the intercept operator began to listen to a conversation and tape record it, would he write anything down immediately on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: If it wasn't necessary or if he couldn't immediately transcribe it, then the operator would write down in a notebook or on a piece of paper which conversations he would later transcribe from the tape so as to make sure not to forget, and so as to avoid anyone else having to listen to the whole tape again. That was the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Very briefly, which types of conversations would be deemed insignificant and irrelevant? If you could just describe a little bit what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Sometimes somebody would be just inquiring about somebody else. It's hard for me to remember anything specific, but this -- these were conversations that didn't affect any kind of operations, material supplies or anything of importance. Sometimes those people had the need to exchange certain personal information. Sometimes we would listen to their conversations with their family members, their wives and so on. In most cases, we didn't consider such conversations to be significant as they were not linked to combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you were listening - you personally - to conversations, how would you try to identify the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: If a conversation flowed, the VRS officer would usually introduce himself. When he's asking for somebody from an operator or to be connected to someone, he would usually introduce himself, and this can be seen from the notebooks or by listening to the conversations. Then during the conversation too, they often addressed themselves, each other, by name. However, if we didn't start to tape from the beginning of the conversation and we were not certain of the voice modulation and we couldn't recognise the voice, then we would mark those participants with numbers, 1, 2, or give them some other sign, but mostly it was numbers. They were participants 1 and 2 which meant that we weren't sure who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said in your answer just now, if we couldn't recognise a voice, were there some voices of officers that you could recognise by your experience of doing this work and listening to many conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. If you hear someone dozens of times, then you will remember his voice. I'm not a phonetics expert but when some of my friends call me, they don't have to introduce themselves. I know by the colour of their voice who they are, and each one of us knows that from experience. So we knew a large number of officers by their voices. We knew exactly who they were without them having to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when these tapes were filled, what happened to the tapes used on the UHER recording machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Once a tape was full, it would be replaced by a new one on the tape recorder. The tape would be put aside until the shift, when the company commander came with the next shift, then the full tape would be carried to the corps command where I assume it may have been listened to again, at least that was the explanation I was given and the other men, and then the tape would be deleted and it would be brought back by the next shift to our location. And we always had several tapes in reserve for us to be able to work normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one question? Private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you a few questions now about the process of transcription of the tapes into the notebooks. You started to talk about that, how if it was urgent it would be transcribed right away and, if not urgent, the operator would do it towards the end of his shift. How would you deal with parts of a tape which were difficult to understand? If the sound quality was not good, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: If the person who is transcribing the conversation from the tape to the notebook is unable to decipher it himself, then the rest of us would help, and several of us would listen to that part of the conversation to be able to decipher that word or several words. If we failed to find out what was said, then we would put down "unrecognisable" or "there is a disturbance," and radio Paket communications, when they have contact among themselves, they would cause a disturbance and this was heard in the receiver. So it could cover a word or two, and then we would put down that we cannot decipher a word or we have disturbances due to these Paket communications. We never allowed ourselves to write down a word that we guessed at, unless we really could understand what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many times would you listen to the tape, if you had to, to make sure that the transcription was accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Sometimes we would try up to ten times, and if we failed, then we would ask someone else to help. And if we just couldn't find out what was said, then we would just write down what I just said. So many times we would re-listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many notebooks were in use at any given time during July 1995? In other words, we have talked about the different operating stations but how many notebooks were there in the room that were being used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Usually only two notebooks would be used because there were only two operators working in a shift. But we always had several notebooks in reserve as well. If there was a need for more notes, if there was a lot of activity in a certain period of time, then we would use as many as were necessary but as a rule there were two that were active. Once one was filled, it would be replaced by another one and put aside until next shift, together with the tapes, and taken to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Without saying his name, would the same person who picked up the tapes pick up the books?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The same person. When there was a change of shift, that is what that person did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also started talking about how after the conversations had been transcribed into a notebook it would be typed up on to the computer and I think you said usually by the intercept operator had transcribed the conversation. During this process of typing the intercept or the conversation into the computer, were any edits made at that stage or is that really just typing what is in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: As far as I know, what was in the notebook would be typed out. I never noticed that any one of the operators had sent a different text or a text in a different form from the one in which it had been written down. There may have been a change of letter but this mustn't or couldn't change the meaning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, when these encrypted reports, the conversations were sent to the 2nd Corps, can you tell me what method, very briefly, of encryption that was? How was it so that it could not be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I've already mentioned the radio or rather the Paket radio, our repeater centre, which means that there is an antenna, a radio transmitter, and the frequency is between 400 -- 140 and 150 megahertz, because we worked with those. Then a modem or interface which adapts the radio transmitter to the computer, and then the computer had its own software for zipping this information and sending it to the command of the 2nd Corps, to another computer there. So it was this Paket communication as it was called because it is actually computers that are communicating and sending brief information, so this brief information, which is called a Paket anywhere in the world, and we called it that, too, and then one computer sends it to another computer through this communication link, and then the computer either confirms that it was received or not, and then it has to be repeated, if necessary. So that's why it's called Pakets, and this information is sent between two computers by way of these small packets that are encrypted, protected, by a system supported by the software we had in the computer itself. We as operators did not really talk. This was digital communication, encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said these were sent towards the end of shifts but how often during a day or during a shift, say, would transmissions be sent, just at the end or at intervals, if you can describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, if it wasn't urgent, if there weren't any major combat actions taking place, if we didn't have to send something straight away, usually we would send it at the end of our shift. However, if there was combat activity or something else, then we would record something and send it further on as fast as possible. If there would be a forward command post then we would send it directly to the forward command post. If not, then we would send it directly to the corps command, and, of course, they acted at their own discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I'd now like to change topics - that's the end of the general description - and talk about some specific intercepts. utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this an intercept that you monitored and recorded or one that you just transcribed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody else would have written up a conversation that I had intercepted. Every conversation I intercepted I wrote up myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think this is pretty obvious but here you've identified the speakers as 1 and 2. Based on what you said before, that's because you didn't know the names of the speakers; is that right? At least as you began writing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's quite right. Because it was actually emphasised here that the conversation did not start from the very beginning, so these were interlocutors who I could not recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll see that if we can -- can we put the English up next to it? Is that possible? What we've got there now on the right is the translation of the printout but it's the same conversation. Just so it's clear what you've just said, we can see on the English on the right next to an asterisk is written, "not from the beginning." I noticed by speaker 2, in your handwritten transcription in the notebook you've drawn just lines rather than any conversation. Does that indicate that you couldn't hear what the person was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, I think it's in the second paragraph here that I wrote, "You cannot hear it." That's what I said, inaudible, you cannot hear it, number 2. And that is why it was marked here at the very outset that you could not hear number 2. And then further on I just put these little lines so there was nothing to be heard. I mean, I couldn't identify the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's on both the B/C/S version on the left and on English on the right but just so we know you've written the number 740.000. That refers to the frequency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. That means that it's a frequency of 740 megahertz, so it is RRU-800. That is the device used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And then on the right, this is also fairly obvious but you've written "1445." What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: 1445 signifies the time when we started intercepting that conversation, the moment when the tape was turned on, on the recording, when the scanning ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back one page on the notebook to 7915. I don't know if we can do that in Sanction. Apparently we can't bring that up in Sanction. If I could put the original notebook on the screen, I'd like to go back one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, if we could put this on the ELMO. Could you just bring it down a little bit so we can see the ERN number? If we could get the whole -- yeah, if it's possible to get the whole page, pull it out a little bit. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, sir, you can look at the book on your right it might be more easy, but do you see the date written there, 13 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I see it. It's on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If you could just turn the page to 7916, and there we see the intercept which you transcribed, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, this date of 13 July 1995, on the previous page, is that related in any way to your intercept that you've transcribed at 1445 on the next page of the book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the date. As you leaf through this notebook, you can see exactly what are the dates involved, although there weren't regular entries on every particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that. Now, if we can go back to the same printout, please, and actually if we could not broadcast this, we shouldn't broadcast the English. We actually shouldn't translate the either the B/C/S or the English outside the courtroom. I can -- I'm told we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I think this is fairly self explanatory, but the top heading, but underneath report, the information, could you very, very briefly just tell us what those different pieces of information mean? You've already explained the frequency and the time. Let me start with at the top it says, RM number 3, in English, and we can blow that up to make it easier, hopefully, for you to read. Would it be better if I gave you a hard copy? Okay. Are you able to read that, sir, where it starts off "zona 2"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: It says, after "zona 2," RM number 3, radio network number 3. And then this is IC, ICOM, R-100, plus ICOM, R-71 E. That's a type of receiver and transmitter. And then RRU-800 is the radio relay network that was intercepted. And then the azimuth is 180, the frequency 740. 02 K means the second channel. I already mentioned that the RRU-800 system involves 24 channels so this particular conversation was recorded on the second channel out of the 24. And the time was 1445.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you've written, participants 1, question mark, and then 2, and then in parentheses, Zoran?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what's written here. I'd like to see the transcript in its entirety because probably at the end, the participant mentioned his own name or the other one called him by his name. Had I known I wouldn't have written number 2. I would have immediately written Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll go to the second page of the transcript, please. And if we can blow up the very bottom line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. It says so very nicely. "Okay, Zoki, bye." Zoki is a nickname for Zoran, a shorter version of Zoran. It couldn't be any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm almost done with this one but if we could -- this is I'm sorry, slightly complicated, Your Honour. If we could go to the B/C/S from the notebook? And if we could also have the B/C/S of this version of the transcript, of the printout? All right, sir, and if you -- this is something we talked about earlier in my office. The section blown up from the notebook is missing from the printout in B/C/S on the right, if we look at the bottom of page 7582 and the top of page 7583, we can see that that section ending at "predaju," is not there. Now, if we could go to this version on the right of the printout, which we looked at earlier, the passage is included. If you know, can you tell me, tell us, why the blown-up passage did not appear on the section we looked at -- at the printout we looked at just a moment ago and does appear on this printout? If you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I assume, as I can see in the way it was printed, that this must be a very old computer, and when the pages were turned over, there must have been this error that occurred. That is my assumption, that that was the reason. Whereas here you have the complete text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. If we could -- I'm not going to go over the intercept at tab 2 in any detail. Could we go to tab 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to know the missing part that he referred to that was on the B/C/S on the screen. Can we have exactly where it begins in English and where it ends? The missing part that was on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good point. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if we can bring the English up? It's starting at the bottom of page 1 of the English, I believe, going through on the top of page 2, to just above, "Well, they reckon that there are about more than a thousand of them." And I can't be completely specific, I'm sorry, it starts in the B/C/S again at "predaju," that is where it starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is this page different from ours? Our page 2 starts with the word, "the spot."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what we see on the screen, on the monitor, is two further lines down, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The monitor starts with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's because we are using a revised translation. It should be in your packets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, there is more than one translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the revised translation, Your Honour. It should read 03204609 ET 2/revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That makes it more confusing. We do have more than one translation, it seems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first translation is the translation of the notebook. And this is the translation of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it should be the revised translation of the report. That's what I'm referring to, as the English which shows --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we only have one translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't have the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure what the Defence has. Or maybe we have the revised one and what we have on the screen is the original one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What's in this book is correct, the one on the screen. The one in the book is the correct one. It should start with "the spot," and I'm sorry we don't have that. That one is apparently not in our system at the moment on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to make things clear both for ourselves and also for the Defence. In other words, can you read out in English, from the revised or the final or the most up-to-date version that you have, which part is missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is the part which begins, at the bottom of page 1 of the revised translation, "Speaker number 1, these guys who were surrendering," starts there. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is that clear enough, Mr. Bourgon? Can we see again on the monitor, please, the corresponding part in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.text: Is that clear, Mr. Bourgon? In other words from the highlighted part in the B/C/S version we need to eliminate the last line from the highlight. utterances.text: The other one. There, at the bottom of the one on the left, 7582, we see at the very bottom the speaker 1 ending with the word "h-v-a-t-a-j-u," and then 2 sort of fades out.
