utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I just want to look because I haven't had a feedback with Mr. Bourgon whether he's happy with this explanation or not because you don't seem either clear in your mind or convinced. I don't know. If we can help you further, Mr. Bourgon, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've got the missing part now but maybe in order to clarify things, it would be good because this was an issue that was raised when this witness testified in the Krstic case, the judges did ask some questions then concerning the differences between the various version that is we have before us now. And maybe my colleague can give the same explanation over again in terms of what was done by ICTY and what really comes from the Bosnian government, because we have different versions here and what we have on the screen, for example, right now, on the right side, is something that was done by ICTY, whereas on the left side is something that comes from the Bosnian government, and I think it's important to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I disagree with that and I don't think it should necessarily be in front of the witness, that type of discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. Anyway, we'll have time to deal with this before you come to the cross-examinations, I suppose. In the meantime, perhaps you can discuss it amongst yourselves. But otherwise, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, I think it's clear enough, at least in my mind; let's put it like this. And it seems with Judge Kwon as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. Nicholls, do you have the page in front of you which is the translation of the notebook? The first page. It's the passage which appears after the sentence, passage starting with, "It's a madhouse." You see the passage missing? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the last sentence it says, "As printed." Are you coming to that or not? "As printed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is the -- as printed is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The parts in brackets are parts that the translators have put in. That's their comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it appear in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. That is not -- that is a translation issue. They have written that, "as printed." That would not appear in the notebook, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is not the translation of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. That is a CLSS insertion, that is their comment on what they have translated. Because wherever you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is, from what did they translate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is from the printout with the missing section, not from the handwritten notebook. That is the translation you were looking at, 00935899.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it is on the screen now, Your Honours, and at the bottom of the translation it has the ERN number of the printout. But just to make it clear, wherever something appears in these back slash brackets, that is something inserted by CLSS. Sometimes they do it if there is an acronym and they spell it out. Sometimes they put a question mark if they are not sure of the word, but that would not be something in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do we have a translation of handwritten note?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We do not, I believe, have a translation of the handwritten notebook. In some of these cases, we have a translation of just one of the versions, whether it's the printout A or the notebook. In some cases we actually have two at the moment. But in this case I believe we do not have one of the notebook and we've put in the best translation available. That's why the updated translation was included although it's unfortunately not yet in the computer system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that intercept. If we could go to intercept tab 4, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're moving, I have one more question. At the end of the handwritten note, did you deal with the date? I don't remember. Whose writing is that, 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can ask the witness and we can bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of this intercept --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness said something there, Your Honour, obviously I didn't understand it and it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we need to have it translated. Mr. Nicholls, perhaps you can ask the witness what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your comment that -- the interpreters did not catch it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: The question was put to me but the text didn't immediately appear on the screen and I was just saying that the text is not on the screen, and I can't give an answer until I see what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you see it now, under where you had written the nickname Zoki, there is a date written there, 14 July, 95; first of all, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I think it is. That is roughly the way I write numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what does that date -- we looked earlier at the date on the preceding page. What does this date at the end of the intercept signify, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: After so much time has gone by, I can't remember, and I wouldn't like to say anything I'm not quite certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, Mr. Nicholls, just to have it clear in my mind? Before you meant to take us to tab 4, to the intercept at tab 4, after having finished with tab 1, at least according to what I have in the transcript, is that you said, "I'm not going to go over the intercept at tab 2 in any detail." Does that mean that you meant to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- into it somewhat, because if you did, you haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I meant was, at the very beginning I asked the witness if he had reviewed that intercept in his handwriting and confirmed that that was a -- one of his intercepts that he recorded and recognised. That was as far as I was going to go and not go into any more detail on that, on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to tab 4, please, and put up the handwritten notebook. And at the same time, could we put up the English translation which we have, which is actually of the printout?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, sir, do you recognise your handwriting on the left page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. That is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, looking at this, take a moment to look at the intercept, can you tell me, it's pretty -- perhaps clear, but how did you identify the speakers in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: They introduced themselves, or they introduced one to another. First it was Mr. Popovic who introduced himself and then General Krstic answered, "Krstic." And then they continue the conversation, and he says, "Yes, boss." So I didn't recognise anything. I just noted what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the printout, please, B/C/S on the left which we have the translation on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this intercept according to the transmission, the report, was frequently 245.950 megahertz. Was that frequency associated by you with any particular units or headquarters or persons, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: In concrete terms, this is the radio relay device RRU-1, working at a lower range, that is from 170 to 260 megahertz. I think I said 230 the first time but I think it's 260 or 280, and here the frequency is 245.950 megahertz. At the time this conversation was recorded, I probably knew exactly which centre this was and what its secret name was, but now I'm unable to say with certainty that it was specifically linked to a particular centre. It is a point through which many other communications pass in various other directions, so the radio relay device was not used by just one person for me to be able to say who the user was of that particular frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. They talk, the participants, in this intercept about -- Krstic says, "Get on over to Bajina Basta." Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. Bajina Basta is in the Republic of Serbia, nowadays the state of Serbia. It is on the other side of the Drina River. It is not in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And azimuth 135, just so we are clear, it states that, that is what direction or where would that be on the face of a clock from your -- from the southern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: If you had a compass in your hand, you know what the north is, so 12.00 would be the north, and 3.00 would be azimuth 30 -- 90, I'm sorry, so this would be southeast in relation to 12.00. In relation to the location where I was, it could be somewhere close to Han Pijesak, Konjevic Polje, or that area. If one had a map, one would be able to indicate exactly what the location is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while we are talking about locations, if you can answer this question as simply as you can, can you tell the location of a speaker, if you don't know who is talking, if it's just 1 and 2, can you tell the location of the speakers just by the frequency? Is that possible or impossible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: No. I think that is impossible because a radio relay centre enables all users from all directions to communicate, like any telephone lines. So someone could have called up from another country. So it is not possible to determine the location solely on the basis of the frequency. Only if a person indicated the name or the name of the unit or the code name, and if the code name was heard, then one would know exactly through which centre the conversation is coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours we are five minutes, I think, from the break, if I have the time correct. This has taken longer than I thought but I will for sure finish today. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have the break now, as per your desire or wish, and we'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, go ahead, please. We'll stop at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going now to the intercept at tab 5. utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, please look at the page on the right, the ERN 01077953. And the lines starting at 245950 below -- well, actually on this whole page, do you recognise your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see that on the right, the conversation which starts on the right page, 7953, the time noted is 1300, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look on the left side, the previous page, which is 7952, we see the intercept we have just been talking about, which has the time noted at 1240, 20 minutes before, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So are these two intercepts that you listened to then and transcribed in sequence as they appear in the book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me just ask you: Besides looking at this book is this an intercept that you remember, that stuck out in your mind in any way, these two intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. I think I will never forget this for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go and have the English translation up on the screen, please. This is 1395. And Your Honours, this is the translation of the printout. The translation of the notebook does appear at the very beginning of this tab. Sorry, could we put the B/C/S up for the witness, of the printout? And we should, I'm sorry, we should, to be on the safe side, not broadcast this, although we can have it on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Make sure that -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the printout on the right, we can see your intercept from 1240 which we've just looked at in the book as well as the next intercept at 1300. Do you see that on the right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at the top heading, on the top left of this page, it says, "Strictly confidential, number 03/0208." Can you tell me what that number means, 03/0208? And if you have trouble reading it, I'll give you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: That number should -- well, 03 should be probably the number of the conversation, and 02 and 08 should be the 2nd of August, the date. So that would mean that it was recorded on the 2nd of August. You can see the date down here, the 2nd of August 1995. Usually that's the way we'd mark documents, with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And would this 030 -- 03/0208, was that typed in by the person operating the computer before this report was sent to headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, of course. I mean, the computer does it and you just correct the date for the next date. So every one that was sent was sent with that letterhead, so to speak, and with the right date and number. That is to say that we, who were transcribing these texts from the tape, we did not enter that. Whoever would copy that from the notebook on to the computer would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and just to be clear, we can see from these two intercepts that the azimuth is the same, 135, and the frequency is the same, 245.950 megahertz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite correct, and it can be seen from this particular case, RRU-1 with its frequency, its azimuth, and the timing, R-3.000 is the device that was used for listening to this frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you -- you've listed the participants here as Krstic and Popovic. How did you -- for this intercept, how did you arrive at their identities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, their identity was established by way of the introductions themselves. There is no denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that we played a tape recording in my office of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to play that now, if we can. It will be on Sanction, and first, though, if we can get the English translation of the tape recording on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask to clarify what is going to be played to us. Is it the original or is it some copy, a copy of the original, or of some other recording? Could we just know what this is exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can you answer that question, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a copy of the original. It's been put into Sanction. The original is in the vault, in the evidence vault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Clear enough, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we -- what he means by exact original. This is not the original recording, obviously, because it's been digitised and fed into the computer but it is a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, we had received information that there were some originals on tapes. We were informed that this was re-recorded on to some other tapes and later on, well, this is a third version of all of this. So that's why I thought it was necessary to clarify the matter. I think that we should see the original, since the Prosecution has it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can make it available to counsel to listen to the actual tape on the special tape recording machine that -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we listen to the original, it will be here in the courtroom. It's no point in making it available to counsel and not to us or other counsel, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's exactly the same, and I note there wasn't any request for this earlier for him -- he could have come by and listened to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls. Let's proceed with what you have now. And if there are -- there is an ad hoc request, please come forward with it, Mr. Zivanovic, and we'll see if it's the case of proceeding accordingly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may say one thing before we play the tape, the -- there is a translation in your packet, and in the Defence packet, it's impossible to put that on the screen while we play the tape and that should be T 0000822 B-ET translation. And let me be very clear. The other printouts we've seen today that I've shown have all been ones we received as evidence. This translation is a transcript made by CLSS of the tape recording. So this is our transcript. Now if we could play the tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before we proceed. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just don't know why we cannot hear the simultaneous interpretation of the recording, not the text. The text is something that we have. I think that we should hear the simultaneous interpretation of the recording itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is impossible. It is impossible to interpret from that kind of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you received this but we've -- the interpreters have just told us that is impossible. It's impossible to interpret from that kind of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My submission Your Honour, also, would be that it's completely unnecessary because that's asking somebody to do an interpretation on the fly as they are listening as opposed to what's been done carefully in a controlled environment where they have been able to listen to it over and over again and get it right. So I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are just making a -- creating a storm in a tea cup. Let's go through it -- with it. Okay? Through with it. Let's listen to it. Now, if you have problems with the translation that has been made available, please come forward, say so, and we'll try and see how we address the problem. Otherwise, I don't see why we shouldn't-- why we should even be discussing these matters. Let's listen to what we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to complicate matters. Could I just inquire whether the Court wishes the interpreters to read out the translation that we have in front of us? Certainly in my previous case, that is what was done on these occasions or whether the Court simply wants us all to hear the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I thought I heard Mr. Nicholls saying previously was that the transcript will appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, if it seems to be -- it's impossible to put the transcript on the screen at the same time that we play the recording. But we all have it in our packets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But the thing is in other words, because I see the point raised, in other words we will be hearing presumably two voices speaking their own language, which we don't understand, and we are not having any simultaneous translation because the interpreters tell us that that is impossible. What we can do is look at the transcript that we have. On the other hand, if we do what you suggested, Mr. Josse, I mean, the interpreters will translate into what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They simply read out what we have in the packet. That is what I've heard them do in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we can read out that ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the reason it was done previously was so that it was on the transcript, Your Honour. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to interfere further. I just simply wanted to clarify the position before we begin the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: I see your point and I think we quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see the point but I want to have it clear in my mind what's going to happen, because presumably the interpreters will read it out in English. Is that going to be translated into B/C/S while the accused and others are listening to the tape in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we need to do is just play the tape and if my friend wants it made part of the record it can be read into the record afterwards but the tape just needs to be played by itself. We can follow along. It's going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that. I'm not requesting that. Let me make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I don't want is anything because we will be hearing voices and not understand anything. I speak for myself. But there may be others, including, and particularly so, the accused themselves, who will be listening to this alleged conversation, and I wouldn't like to have anything interfere with their listening and with their following the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't know. I am a little bit torn between what Mr. Josse has suggested, which makes a lot of sense, and the practical approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a very short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed this way, because I think Mr. Josse is right. Let's have the tape played and the interpreters will, at least for the purpose of the transcript, read out what they have available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, could we just play it twice then so that there is no cross interpretation or any interference? It's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The translation will take place only in English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the accused can follow the real tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And they will -- the quality of the audio, they will have to follow along and just read off of the translation. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can listen -- listen to it once, I think that should be enough. I don't think we need to play it twice. If -- whoever is going to follow in the Serbian-Croat language just has to make sure that they focus on that channel and on nothing else because otherwise it will get confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It will just be extremely difficult to impossible. Even with the best quality, if the interpreters do not have a transcript, I don't believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not the interpreters -- the interpreters will read the transcript and, if there is any translation issues, they can be raised later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can proceed along these lines. So you play the tape, the interpreters read out slowly the transcript so that we have it in the record. Okay, and then if -- we'll see what the position will be afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have an exact reference which transcript will be read out, out of the three under tab 5? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is T 0000822 B-ET/translation. It's towards the back of the packet. It is not the one which states draft translation. It's the final translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Got it? Got it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that we do not have that kind of numbering -- THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: The French booth: We do not have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- 822 B-ET/translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to provide the interpreters with this document. It's this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's play the tape and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that being so. THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: The French booth interpreters note we will have to translates from English into French because we do not have the documents in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are -- the English booth is not going to have the document in English either. In other words we are not going to have any translations at all. We are just proceeding with the playback of the recording and that will be it for the time being. Because otherwise it's getting too complicated. And as far as the record goes, I think we can find a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The English booth does have that particular transcript if you wish to have it read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are not going to have anything read out while the playback is ongoing. Is it clear? And the transcript will only show that this recording was played from such time to such time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, if we could play it now from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, were you able to hear -- sir, were you able to follow that tape-recorded conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that the same conversation which you monitored at 1300 hours on the 2nd of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that you transcribed into the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could bring back up the English, please, of the report, and the B/C/S of the report, and it's down at the bottom on your right, sir, in your language. You can see that the conversation as recorded starts, "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Krstic and then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Stop, please. I have nothing on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is right, because -- all right. Do you have the two pages now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look, sir, at the bottom of the page on your right, that transcript of the intercept at 1300, which begins: "K: Molim? And then "P: Sefe." In English, "Yes." And "Hey, boss." That is how you have started to transcribe the conversation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go, I think just the English of the transcript of the tape recording on the right. Again it is our transcript of the tape. There is a little bit more on the transcript of the tape, sir. We have "P: Hey boss. And then"Y: Just a minute. "P: Popovic here. "Y: Hey, what's up, go ahead. "P: Is Uran there? In person? "Y: ... couldn't hear. And then "P: I need to talk to Krle, Krle." Did you hear that exchange they beginning of the tape we listened to when you were listening to it in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that a moment ago on the tape, and I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, my question is: This little extra part of the tape, why did you not transcribe that into the notebook and into your report, that little portion where P says "Popovic here"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I didn't consider that part necessary because it relates to the conversation between Mr. Popovic and the operator on duty, who just needs to connect him to his boss. And when he asked, "Is Uran there, not Zoran" that was the code name of his boss. And I didn't consider this to be significant because this was just a way of getting -- establishing contact between operators in radio relay systems. I don't think that it is worth devoting special attention to. However, now, listening to the tape, one can hear this part of the conversation that we now see in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Who is going first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One housekeeping question, Mr. Nicholls. In relation to the 65 ter number, the index says this is 65 number 1395 but actually I found you put A or Bs at the end of the numbers and I -- it was difficult -- impossible to find -- for me to find the document with this number so could you clarify the number in general? When do you put A or B?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That, and I might have to get some help from my colleague, the intercept has one number, 1395, and then because there are printouts, audio, handwritten notebooks and translations, those all have subnumbers, so the index we can provide a better index which says which is which. For example 1395 D is the translation of the handwritten notebook. 1395 D should bring up the notebook in e-court and then the translation will be attached. 1395 B is the printout and the translation should be attached to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the rest have other numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon and thank you, Mr. Nicholls. I understand Mr. Zivanovic for Colonel Popovic is going first. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in this southern facility, I won't mention the name, as we agreed, in addition to the platoon which you were the leader, was there any other unit present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes. There was the communications squad of three or four men, I already said, who engaged in their own activities regarding communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did your unit have any functional connection with that communications unit? In other words, was your work linked to this communications unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: No. It was not linked to that unit in any way. It is a separate unit of the corps. They had their own duties and activities that we did not interfere with, neither did they interfere in ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to monitoring enemy communications, did you engage in any other activities linked to counter-electronic combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: From this facility that I was in command of, we only intercepted conversations on these radio relay devices; at times other frequencies were monitored as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your unit engage in encryption of the data that was being forwarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation. Our unit did not do the encrypting. It was done by the software in the computer so we didn't need any personnel for encrypting or for coding, but once the text was typed in, which we had transcribed from the tape, then the computer itself produces its own hieroglyphics and this then goes on to the computer it is linked to which has the same software and then this other computer reads it back in text form in the way it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that by automatically entering a text into your computer, it was automatically encrypted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, yes. Literally. But in principle, the text would first be typed out and then you set the software in motion for the computer protected so it wasn't automatically done as one types it into the computer but once it was typed in, instructions would be given to the computer to encrypt it and then through Paket links this would be forwarded in the form of small packets to the other computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that each member of the platoon could do this, enter the text into the computer, and give instructions for the text to be encrypted and then forwarded to another unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: In principle, the actual link between the corps was established by one operator. We would type in our text into the computer in the form we had transcribed it in, but the rest was done by an operator who was equipped for this, who was specialised in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say processing, you mean sending the encrypted text to your higher unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: When I say processing, that means giving the instruction to the computer to encrypt it and then send it on. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your work engage in jamming enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: If I'm talking only about my platoon, for a period of time we did make some attempts at that, but we didn't have the necessary equipment, so that we did very little of that, because jamming such information and that kind of links, I don't think, has any logic or meaning. And if we tried sometimes to do some jamming, it was usually simply as a trial on civilian communications because these radio relay devices had channels for the transfer of civilian communications so that civilians could also enter into communication with their relatives or friends. So that at least my squad did not engage in jamming of this type of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you jammed civilian communications or some others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: This was done experimentally only but in my opinion, it was negligible, it was just an attempt. Because to be able to do jamming, you had to have more powerful radio devices because it is not possible to enter telephone lines. You have to jam with the help of signals and we didn't have such devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at Defence Exhibit 1D75? We only have the B/C/S version. We have asked for all these documents to be translated and we expect them to be done shortly so that we will have them in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This should maybe not be transmitted outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how the questioning is going to go but it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. Okay. No broadcast of the image of this document, all right? Go ahead, and please avoid mentioning the station location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see at the bottom of the screen there is a paragraph which says, "We are jamming because on this channel their teleprinter is operating." It was at the bottom. Now it's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it says, "We are jamming because their teleprinter is working on this channel. Previously we jammed the teleprinter on RRU-1, 264.975 frequency and 252.375 frequency successfully. We assume that they have shifted from RRU-1 to RUP-12." I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: This is something unknown to me but I can explain what I know about it. If we follow the report, this is a frequency between 30 and 70 megahertz that my department never monitored or jammed anyone. This is work done probably by the radio communications department and I have already said that I really don't know what they were doing. And if they did this, according to this text, this jamming, that is something I really don't know. My unit did not engage in that. I can say that with full responsibility. But it could have been this other department, if you're talking about my facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have many other documents from which we see that from this location, such jamming was done. I'm interested in learning whether you had any indications, whether anyone told you that a unit right next to you, very close to you, in your immediate vicinity, is jamming communications? Is it possible for this to be happening without you not knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: All I can say is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt so early but he has answered that. He said he didn't know what they were doing and he was just looking at this and speculating because he didn't know what they were doing, this other unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nicholls is right because basically however many excerpts you can refer him to from the various documents that you have in your possession, I think the answer, you have it already, and it's not going to change so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have found another document which says - and I can show it to you, but that may not be necessary - that there were certain zones that your unit monitored. And there four zones according to what I saw. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I can just say not that -- not only do I not remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could counsel just tell me which document he's talking about on his list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Which document are you referring the witness to or you are referring to anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime I think the witness indicated that he is not in a position to answer this question. Do you want to have a look at this document or do you think you can proceed to answer this question without the need to refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just, with respect to zones, say that in every printed transcript with a header, the zone is indicated. So these zones did exist. But I cannot now, nor did I know at the time, which is which zone. This was up to the command. When we received an order, they would say, zone such and such, frequency such and such, and you are expected to monitor that azimuth and that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that your unit had a maximum of nine men. If I understood you correctly, you worked in shifts. So half of the unit would go to this southern facility, to call it that, whereas the other half would stay wherever they stayed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't understand one another. My unit, which I was the commander, consisted of two squads, with a maximum of eight to nine men in each. Usually there were nine of us. So those nine were always present in one shift. And then 10 days or 15 days later, the next squad would come with nine men, and that is how we worked. So there were always enough of us to cover four shifts with two men each. Sometimes, when necessary, when there were combat operations, we had no working hours or anything, we were all on duty all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that there was a unit in the north. I don't want to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it more numerous than yours or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think it was, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How long was one shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: It usually lasted six hours. Usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're talking about the day-time shift. I'm talking about the shift when you go to the facility and stay there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Oh, I see. We would stay there for 10 days and in winter time, when it was difficult to go on foot, as we had to, then the shift would last 15 days. We would have a change of shift every 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please -- let's just summarise. In answer to a question of the Prosecution, you described the equipment that you had, that you had receivers, tape recorders. You showed us the photographs. And we saw all that equipment, including the computer which was very important for you. Tell us, what was the condition of this equipment? What condition was it in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Most of the equipment at the time when we were working was new. The receivers, R-100 that I mentioned, AOR-3000 that was mentioned a moments ago, all these were new devices, which, I really don't know through which channels they reached us, and reached our units. I don't know. Probably from abroad. I just -- I don't know. A part of the equipment at the beginning, in 1992, or most of the equipment, was from radio clubs, from my radio club. We used all the equipment that we had for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which of the equipment was new?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, answer this question, and then we wind up for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned just now the radio receiver ICOM R-100. Then radio receiver AOR-3000, also new. Then the shortwave receiver and transmitter, Kenwood, was also new. The tape recorders were not new because they were collected from various companies because they were used for recording meetings of workers councils and the tapes were, were from there, too, then some other shortwave devices were new. There was one mentioned in a transcript, ICOM CR-71. This is also a shortwave receiver, so all the equipment was new except for the tape recorders. Part of the antennas we found there when we arrived. Some of them we made ourselves. The converters that used to reduce the frequency we made ourselves. I made some of them myself for us to be able to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. And the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: The computer we all had computers at home even before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was, was it new?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. I thank you, Witness. We will reconvene tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Thank you. In the meantime, Witness, you are not to communicate with anyone or let anyone communicate with you on the matters you're testifying upon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
